A few months ago, I found myself drowning in research papers. As someone working in AI/ML, I constantly need to reference academic papers, technical documentation,…
That's when I decided to build something that could change how I interact with documents. Not just another PDF reader, but an intelligent assistant that could…
The idea seemed simple: upload a PDF, ask questions, get answers. But as I dug deeper, I realized this involved some fascinating technical challenges:
How do you break down a document so an AI can understand it?
How do you find the most relevant parts when someone asks a question?
How do you keep everything private and running locally?
How do you make the responses actually useful, not just generic?
These questions led me down the rabbit hole of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) - a technique that combines information retrieval with language generation.
RAG was a game-changer for me. Instead of trying to stuff entire documents into an AI model (which doesn't work well), RAG breaks the problem into two parts:
Generation: Use those pieces to generate a helpful response
Think of it like having a really smart research assistant. When you ask a question, they first go through all your documents to find the relevant sections, then use…

When you ask "What are the main findings?", it doesn't just look for documents containing those exact words. Instead, it converts your question into a mathematical…

I used Mistral 7B Instruct through llama.cpp, which lets you run powerful language models locally. The key was using quantized models - they're smaller and faster…

The key insight was making the RAG parameters configurable. Different documents work better with different settings:
Research papers might need larger chunks to preserve context
Legal documents might need more retrieved results for comprehensive answers
Users can adjust chunk size, number of results, and search mode in real-time and see how it affects their results.
Building DocTract taught me that RAG isn't just about the technology - it's about understanding how people actually want to interact with information.
Context is everything: The quality of your chunks determines the quality of your answers
Retrieval is as important as generation: If you can't find the right information, even the best LLM can't help
User control matters: Different documents and use cases need different approaches
Local deployment is viable: You don't need cloud APIs for powerful AI applications

This project taught me that MLOps is fundamentally about bridging the gap between data science experimentation and production software engineering. Here are the key…
In traditional data science, the model is everything. In MLOps, the model is just one piece of a larger system that includes data pipelines, APIs, monitoring, and…
Every aspect of your system should be reproducible. This means:
Version control: Not just for code, but for data and models too
Building the API first forces you to think about:
Contract definition: What inputs and outputs does your system need?
Error handling: How do you gracefully handle edge cases?
Production systems need monitoring, logging, and alerting. This isn't an afterthought - it's a core requirement.
MLOps systems should be designed to learn and improve over time through:
Through this project, I discovered several principles that apply to any ML system:
Assume external APIs will be down, models will drift, and containers will crash. Build resilience into your system from the start.
You can't improve what you can't measure. Instrument your system with metrics, logs, and health checks.
Complex systems are hard to debug, deploy, and maintain. Start simple and add complexity only when necessary.
APIs, data schemas, and model interfaces are contracts. Design them carefully because changing them later is expensive.
Manual processes don't scale and are error-prone. Automate testing, deployment, and monitoring from the beginning.

Most agent tutorials pick the model. You give a language model a task and a list of tools, and it decides which tool to call, looks at the result, and decides again.…
For mine it wasn't. A compliance check has steps that must happen every time, in a fixed order. Some decisions belong to a person, not to a model. And an audit…
This pattern is often called ReAct (reason, then act). Its strength is flexibility. A research assistant or a coding helper can't know its steps in advance, so the…
But that flexibility cuts both ways. The model can skip a step, call the same tool five times, or stop early because it feels confident. Nothing in this loop makes it…
The loop also has nowhere to stop. If a person has to approve something halfway through, there's no clean place to wait: the loop is just a function running in…
LangGraph describes your agent as a graph, a word that sounds more mathematical than it is. There are three parts:
State: a shared notebook that every step can read and write. In my agent, that's the listing, the problems found and the draft report.
Nodes: the steps. Each one is an ordinary Python function that takes the state and returns the parts it wants to change.
Edges: the arrows between steps, which say what comes next.
If a loop is a chef improvising, a graph is the recipe card. The chef still does the cooking, but the order of the steps is written down.
A few things worth noticing. The nodes don't know about each other; they only read and update the state. Each node returns just the keys it changes, and LangGraph…
A graph doesn't have to be a straight line. A conditional edge is a small function that looks at the state and picks the next step:
This is where the design gets interesting. In my agent, code decides the route. If the checks find nothing, the listing goes straight to its report and the model is…
Loops are still allowed, they just have limits. The step that searches the law can go round at most three times. The step that writes the report is followed by a…
This is the feature that sold me. Inside any node you can call interrupt(), and the graph stops right there. Whatever you pass to it goes to the outside world, for…
First, pausing needs a checkpointer (more on that below) and a threadid, which is simply the name of this particular run. Every audit gets its own.
Second, when the graph resumes, the paused node starts again from its first line, not from the interrupt() call. So anything that runs before interrupt() in that node…
In my agent the review node also checks the answer. If a reviewer rejects a finding without giving a reason, the node calls interrupt() again with the error, and the…
A checkpointer saves the state of each thread to storage. InMemorySaver is perfect for tests and notebooks. For anything real, you swap in a database:
Now a paused audit is just a few rows in Postgres. I can stop the API, deploy a new version and start it again, and the same audits are still waiting for review,…
You can also choose how often it saves. By default LangGraph saves after every step, so a crash in the middle of a run loses almost nothing. My audits take about 20…
I like LangGraph, but it adds weight: a framework, a state schema and a new way of thinking about your code. You probably don't need it if:
your app makes one model call, or a fixed chain of calls with no branches,
nothing ever has to wait for a person, and
runs are short, and losing one is no big deal.
In those cases a plain function is easier to read and easier to debug.
A graph earns its place when you have branches and loops you want to control, a person in the loop, work that must survive a restart, or when you want to watch every…

A few weeks ago, I discovered something that completely changed how I think about AI applications. It is called the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard…
Check your GitHub repositories and analyze code quality in real-time
Query your databases and generate insights from live data
Access your file system and understand your project structure
Monitor your system logs and alert you to issues
All through a single, standardized protocol. That's the power of MCP.
Note: MCP is new and still evolving, adoption is underway, but the protocol specification is not yet finalized. Expect changes as the ecosystem matures.
Before MCP, if you wanted an AI to help with your development workflow, you had two frustrating options:
Copy-paste code snippets, error logs, and documentation into your AI chat. The problems? Information gets outdated quickly, you hit context limits, and the AI can't…
Build specific connectors for each tool you use. Want your AI to check GitHub? Build a GitHub integration. Need database access? Build another integration. This…
MCP introduces a revolutionary third way: a standardized protocol that lets AI assistants connect to any tool or data source via a common interface. Instead of…
MCP client (the AI assistant). Claude, GPT or any other AI system that supports MCP. The client doesn't need to know anything about your specific tools; it only needs…
MCP server (the bridge). Exposes your tools and data through standardized endpoints, and translates between the AI's requests and your actual systems.
Tools and resources (your actual systems). Databases, APIs, file systems, monitoring tools: anything you want the AI to access or control.
Not all MCP implementations support prompt primitives natively yet, but this is an emerging trend in protocol design.
Let's build a practical MCP server that gives AI assistants access to file system operations.
Note: Code examples in this article use simplified syntax for clarity and understanding. Actual implementations may use FastMCP or other specific libraries with…
This server gives any MCP client file system capabilities. An AI can now:
Example functions are for illustration only, production deployments require robust security and error-handling!
(Actual implementations should enforce authentication, authorization, and safe query execution in production.)
Production-grade MCP must enforce authentication, authorization, and secure sandboxing for all AI-driven access and actions.
Multi-modal capabilities: Handling text, images, audio, and video (still experimental in most open-source implementations).
Collaborative AI workflows: Multiple AI assistants working together through MCP.
Real-time streaming: Enabling live data feeds via MCP for continuous monitoring and alerting.
Ecosystem marketplace: A standard protocol accelerates third-party tool/plugin ecosystems, enabling new business and innovation opportunities.
MCP is still an emerging standard and the specification may evolve.
Real-world deployments must implement authentication, authorization, and secure sandboxing to prevent abuse.
Not all existing tools can connect directly; some may require adapters.
Multi-modal support (images, audio, video) is experimental and not widely supported yet.
Always apply rigorous error handling and guardrails, especially for destructive operations.
MCP represents a fundamental shift in how we think about AI tool integration. Instead of building isolated AI applications, we are creating an ecosystem where AI…
The future of AI is not just about better models, it is about better integration. And MCP is leading the way.

Mono vs. stereo: Speech recognition typically uses single-channel audio
Normalization is crucial: Audio levels need to be consistent

Each step is crucial - skip normalization and you get poor results, use the wrong sample rate and the model fails completely.

The Hubert model uses self-supervised learning, which means it learned speech patterns from unlabeled audio data. This approach has several advantages:

The best AI model can't fix bad audio. I learned to:

The combination of pre-trained models, easy-to-use APIs, and excellent documentation makes building AI applications accessible to any developer.
